To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have proposed a method that can be used to adjust survival curves in the setting where there is unmeasured confounder.

we propose a new method for estimating the causal difference in survival curves in observational data, which is based on the instrumental variable estimation of the survival time distribution and a novel procedure for mapping the results onto the survival probability or the expected survival time scale.
we have developed a new procedure for adjusting for unmeasured confounds in survival analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) How to adjust survival curves to the population at risk in the presence of measured covariates and unmeasured ones?

the following: (1) developing a new method for estimating the survival curve in the presence of both measured and unmeased confounders and (2) developing methods for mapping the estimates onto the survival curve and the expected survival scales.

the following questions: (1) How to obtain the causal difference in survival curves when unmeasured confounder are present? and (2) What is the impact on the causal difference in the survival curves when unobserved confounders are present?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method provides a novel way to estimate the causal effect on survival curves in observational studies in the presence of measured and unobserved confounders.
, in the presence of a strong unmeasured confounder, the estimated survival curves are biased and should not be used to make inferences about the population at risk.
the proposed methodology provides an alternative way to summarize the causal effect in terms of survival probabilities and the expected survival times.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new method for estimating the causal impact of a treatment on survival time in the presence of measured and unobserved confounding.
our approach provides a methodological framework to estimate and visualize differences in survival curves when the data are subject to unmeasured confounder effects.
we provide a method for adjusting for the effects of unmeasured covariates on the survival curves in the case of time dependent instrumental variables.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the difference among the expected survival curves for a given treatment can be estimated even in the presence of a large number of unmeasured covariates, provided that the instrumental variable assumptions are met.
, when the unmeasured confounder is present, the difference in the survival curves between treatment arms is biased.
it is possible to adjust survival curves in a semi parametric fashion for unmeasured confounds and that this adjustment is consistent and asymptotically efficient.
